Cluster interpretation relies on manual inspection.
future_direction: Develop more automated approaches for cluster interpretation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often display overconfidence, presenting information with unwarranted certainty in high-stakes contexts. We investigate the internal basis of this behavior via mechanistic interpretability. Using open-sourced Llama 3.2 models fine-tuned on human annotated assertiveness datasets, we extract residual activations across all layers, and compute similarity metrics to localize assertive representations. Our analysis identifies layers most sensitive to assertiveness contrasts and reveals that high-assertive representations decompose into two orthogonal sub-components of emotional and logical clusters-paralleling the dual-route Elaboration Likelihood Model in Psychology. Steering vectors derived from these sub-components show distinct causal effects: emotional vectors broadly influence prediction accuracy, while logical vectors exert more localized effects. These findings provide mechanistic evidence for the multi-component structure of LLM assertiveness and highlight avenues for mitigating overconfident behavior.

papers.title: Steering Language Model Refusal with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can amplifying sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that mediate refusal improve language model safety at inference time, and what are the trade-offs with general model capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: SAE-based feature steering can improve refusal rates for unsafe prompts but introduces a systematic trade-off, degrading performance on safe prompts and general capability benchmarks, indicating deep entanglement between safety-relevant features and general language abilities.
papers.conclusion: While SAE-based feature steering is a promising, flexible approach for enhancing language model safety without retraining, its practical deployment is limited by significant trade-offs with general capabilities, highlighting the need to better understand and address feature entanglement.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal-mediating features can be identified using a simple, handcrafted prompt.
Amplifying identified SAE features (e.g., Feature 22373) increases refusal rates for unsafe prompts in both single-turn and multi-turn jailbreak settings.
This safety improvement comes with increased over-refusal on safe prompts.
Feature steering causes significant regression in factual recall (MMLU, TruthfulQA) and reasoning (GSM8K) performance, even on benign content.
Performance regressions are not unique to safety features; steering a non-safety feature (Feature 216 for philosophy) also degrades capabilities, suggesting a general limitation of the steering approach.
papers.limitation:
The feature identification method is not scalable, relying on a single handcrafted prompt.
Feature steering introduces a trade-off between improved safety and degraded performance on unrelated capabilities.
future_direction: Developing better methods for identifying features that mediate target behaviors.
Understanding why features are entangled with unrelated capabilities and how to isolate them.
Exploring conditional steering approaches that activate interventions only when needed.
papers.abstract: Responsible deployment of language models requires mechanisms for refusing unsafe prompts while preserving model performance. While most approaches modify model weights through additional training, we explore an alternative: steering model activations at inference time via amplifying sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that mediate refusal. This work uncovers a fundamental tension between SAE steering-based safety improvements and general model capabilities. While feature steering successfully improves robustness against both single-turn and challenging multi-turn jailbreak attempts, we discover that this comes at a previously underexplored cost -- systematic degradation of performance across multiple benchmark tasks, even on safe inputs with no apparent connection to refusal behavior. This suggests that features mediating refusal may be more deeply entangled with general language model capabilities than previously understood. Our findings reveal important open questions about the nature of safety-relevant features in language models and the feasibility of isolating them for targeted intervention. While SAE-based steering shows promise as a flexible approach to enhancing language model safety, our results highlight the critical need to understand and address the mechanisms behind these capability tradeoffs before such techniques can be practically deployed.

papers.title: Scaling laws for activation steering with Llama 2 models and refusal mechanisms
papers.research_question: How does the effectiveness of the Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) steering technique scale with model size, specifically for controlling refusal behavior in Llama 2 models?
papers.core_contribution: The effectiveness of Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) for steering model behavior diminishes with increasing model size, negative steering is more effective than positive steering, and steering is most effective when applied at early-mid layers.
papers.conclusion: Model alignment is complex and requires nuanced approaches to steer models effectively as they become larger, with future research needed to understand the interplay between alignment strategies, model architecture, and dataset characteristics.
papers.key_findings:
CAA is most effective when applied at early-mid layers (approximately 0.4 × total layer count).
The effectiveness of CAA diminishes with model size, making larger models harder to steer with the same vectors.
Negative steering (towards non-refusal) has more pronounced effects than positive steering across all model sizes.
The layer of peak steering effectiveness for positive and negative steering converges as model size increases.
The diminishing effectiveness might be because larger models 'drown out' the steering vector due to more downstream computation.
papers.limitation: The experiments were limited to the specific topic of refusal and the results may be different for different topics or prompting approaches.
future_direction: Feature steering with sparse autoencoders (SAE).
Modifying activation steering for larger models, e.g., scaling up steering vectors or injecting at multiple layers.
Experimenting with diverse model architectures (e.g., Mistral, BERT, BLOOM) to understand alignment differences.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) evolve in complexity and capability, the efficacy of less widely deployed alignment techniques are uncertain. Building on previous work on activation steering and contrastive activation addition (CAA), this paper explores the effectiveness of CAA with model scale using the family of Llama 2 models (7B, 13B, and 70B). CAA works by finding desirable 'directions' in the model's residual stream vector space using contrastive pairs (for example, hate to love) and adding this direction to the residual stream during the forward pass. It directly manipulates the residual stream and aims to extract features from language models to better control their outputs. Using answer matching questions centered around the refusal behavior, we found that 1) CAA is most effective when applied at early-mid layers. 2) The effectiveness of CAA diminishes with model size. 3) Negative steering has more pronounced effects than positive steering across all model sizes.

papers.title: Language Models Understand Us, Poorly
papers.research_question: What does it mean for language models to understand human language, and do current and future models achieve such understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Argues that internal representations are sufficient for language understanding, critiques the Scaling Paradigm, and advocates for probing model internals to advance the science of understanding.
papers.conclusion: Current language models have limited understanding due to under-specified data, and scaling alone may not suffice without focusing on internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Understanding-as-representation is sufficient for language understanding, while as-reliability is necessary but not sufficient.
Current language models are limited by under-specification of meaning in their training data.
The Scaling Paradigm may be computationally infeasible for achieving human-like understanding.
Probing model internals is essential to advance the science of understanding.
Adding more modalities and human language aspects is needed for better models.
papers.limitation: The paper presents only one perspective and may not fully cover diverse fields or be ultimately correct.
future_direction: Probe model internals
Add more of human language such as intersubjective, multi-agent environments
Measure what models can learn
papers.abstract: Some claim language models understand us. Others won’t hear it. To clarify, I investigate three views of human language understanding: as-mapping, as-reliability and as-representation. I argue that while behavioral reliability is necessary for understanding, internal representations are sufficient; they climb the right hill. I review state-of-the-art language and multi-modal models: they are pragmatically challenged by under-specification of form. I question the Scaling Paradigm: limits on resources may prohibit scaled-up models from approaching understanding. Last, I describe how as-representation advances a science of understanding. We need work which probes model internals, adds more of human language, and measures what models can learn.

papers.title: From Directions to Cones: Exploring Multidimensional Representations of Propositional Facts in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does truth in LLMs have a multi-dimensional representation (concept cone) rather than a single linear direction, and can such cones causally mediate truth-related behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that truth in LLMs is represented as a multi-dimensional cone in activation space, and that interventions using these cones can reliably steer model outputs on true/false propositions while preserving unrelated capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Multi-dimensional concept cones can reliably steer LLM behavior on true/false propositions across architectures and sizes, revealing a robust subspace of activation vectors that modulate factuality.
papers.key_findings:
Truth-related directions are localized in middle to later layers, with the final token position being most effective for interventions.
Multi-dimensional concept cones for truth exist and can causally mediate truthful behavior across different model families and sizes.
Increasing cone dimensionality generally improves steering effectiveness, but beyond a point, ASR declines, especially in smaller models.
The discovered truth directions are specific and do not significantly affect general instruction-following capabilities (low KL divergence on Alpaca).
The classic DIM direction aligns only with the first axis of the cone; other axes are orthogonal, indicating additional structure.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on relatively small open-source models (1.5B–7B parameters) and may not generalize to larger frontier models.
The operationalization of truth is narrow, limited to simple unambiguous propositional facts, and does not capture more complex notions of truth.
The method does not guarantee discovery of a maximally informative or interpretable subspace, and individual cone axes lack semantic meaning.
future_direction: Pair cones with automated clustering or sparse autoencoding to assign semantic meaning to basis vectors.
Extend the method to larger, instruction-tuned models.
Extend to multimodal settings.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong conversational abilities but often generate falsehoods. Prior work suggests that the truthfulness of simple propositions can be represented as a single linear direction in a model's internal activations, but this may not fully capture its underlying geometry. In this work, we extend the concept cone framework, recently introduced for modeling refusal, to the domain of truth. We identify multi-dimensional cones that causally mediate truth-related behavior across multiple LLM families. Our results are supported by three lines of evidence: (i) causal interventions reliably flip model responses to factual statements, (ii) learned cones generalize across model architectures, and (iii) cone-based interventions preserve unrelated model behavior. These findings reveal the richer, multidirectional structure governing simple true/false propositions in LLMs and highlight concept cones as a promising tool for probing abstract behaviors.

papers.title: Data-efficient Meta-models for Evaluation of Context-based Questions and Answers in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can training data requirements be reduced for state-of-the-art hallucination detection frameworks while maintaining competitive performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a data-efficient framework for hallucination detection that combines feature extraction from LLM internals with lightweight classifiers, achieving competitive performance with only 250 training samples.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that lightweight, annotation-efficient approaches can achieve competitive performance for hallucination detection in industrial settings, overcoming constraints of limited data, computational cost, and privacy.
papers.key_findings:
Lightweight methods using internal LLM states can achieve competitive hallucination detection performance with limited training data.
TabPFNv2 is the top-performing meta-classifier in low-data settings, outperforming logistic regression and CatBoost on average.
PCA dimensionality reduction often enhances the performance of lookback features compared to UMAP or raw features.
Performance improves sharply with 50-250 training samples and plateaus thereafter, demonstrating high data-efficiency.
The choice of extractor LLM affects detector performance, with Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B generally outperforming Gemma-2-9B.
future_direction: Explore architectural modifications of tabular foundation models like TabPFNv2 for NLP representation learning and hallucination detection tasks.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are increasingly deployed in industry applications, yet their reliability remains hampered by challenges in detecting hallucinations. While supervised state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods that leverage LLM hidden states -- such as activation tracing and representation analysis -- show promise, their dependence on extensively annotated datasets limits scalability in real-world applications. This paper addresses the critical bottleneck of data annotation by investigating the feasibility of reducing training data requirements for two SOTA hallucination detection frameworks: Lookback Lens, which analyzes attention head dynamics, and probing-based approaches, which decode internal model representations. We propose a methodology combining efficient classification algorithms with dimensionality reduction techniques to minimize sample size demands while maintaining competitive performance. Evaluations on standardized question-answering RAG benchmarks show that our approach achieves performance comparable to strong proprietary LLM-based baselines with only 250 training samples. These results highlight the potential of lightweight, data-efficient paradigms for industrial deployment, particularly in annotation-constrained scenarios.

papers.title: Caught in the Act: a mechanistic approach to detecting deception
papers.research_question: Can linear probes on LLM internal activations detect deception in generated responses, and how does this capability vary with model size?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on LLM internal activations can detect deception with high accuracy, and larger models contain more distinct deception-related directions in their residual streams.
papers.conclusion: Linear probes are an effective white-box method for detecting deception in LLMs, with performance scaling with model size, and future work should focus on stronger models and more naturalistic scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes achieve >90% accuracy in distinguishing deceptive from non-deceptive arguments for some models (e.g., DeepSeek 7B).
Probe accuracy strongly correlates with model size, with smaller models (1.5B) at chance and larger models (>7B) reaching 70-90%.
Layer-wise probe accuracy follows a three-stage pattern: near-random in early layers, peaking in middle layers, and slightly declining in later layers.
Iterative nullspace projection reveals multiple linear directions encoding deception, ranging from 20 in Qwen 3B to nearly 100 in DeepSeek 7B and Qwen 14B.
LLM-as-judge (black-box) methods show a performance gap of 10-20% between GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini.
papers.limitation:
The dataset struggles to bridge the gap between controlled experimental conditions and real-world deceptive behavior.
LLM-as-judge methods may not scale to more capable future systems that could generate increasingly complex outputs.
Eliciting deception by soliciting incorrect arguments may not capture true deception, as models arguably lack intentionality, and the approach is heavily influenced by explicit prompting.
future_direction: Improving external validity by developing naturalistic scenarios that better reflect real-world deceptive interactions.
Establishing scaling properties of deception detection capabilities.
Incorporating information about the underlying problem distribution to improve the reliability of deception detection.
papers.abstract: Sophisticated instrumentation for AI systems might have indicators that signal misalignment from human values, not unlike a "check engine" light in cars. One such indicator of misalignment is deceptiveness in generated responses. Future AI instrumentation may have the ability to detect when an LLM generates deceptive responses while reasoning about seemingly plausible but incorrect answers to factual questions. In this work, we demonstrate that linear probes on LLMs internal activations can detect deception in their responses with extremely high accuracy. Our probes reach a maximum of greater than 90% accuracy in distinguishing between deceptive and non-deceptive arguments generated by llama and qwen models ranging from 1.5B to 14B parameters, including their DeepSeek-r1 finetuned variants. We observe that probes on smaller models (1.5B) achieve chance accuracy at detecting deception, while larger models (greater than 7B) reach 70-80%, with their reasoning counterparts exceeding 90%. The layer-wise probe accuracy follows a three-stage pattern across layers: near-random (50%) in early layers, peaking in middle layers, and slightly declining in later layers. Furthermore, using an iterative null space projection approach, we find multitudes of linear directions that encode deception, ranging from 20 in Qwen 3B to nearly 100 in DeepSeek 7B and Qwen 14B models.

papers.title: Toward Better Generalisation in Uncertainty Estimators: Leveraging Data-Agnostic Features
papers.research_question: Can supplementing hidden-state features with data-agnostic features improve the probe’s generalisation to unseen tasks or datasets? Does pruning to the top-ranked hidden-state features amplify this generalisation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper investigates whether incorporating data-agnostic features (probability- and entropy-based metrics) with hidden-state features improves the generalization of uncertainty estimators across tasks and datasets, and whether feature selection on hidden states amplifies this effect.
papers.conclusion: Integrating data-agnostic features with hidden-state features can enhance the generalization of uncertainty estimators, and feature selection can amplify this effect, but the approach underperforms on certain transfer pairs, particularly involving Commonsense Reasoning datasets, where the probe fails to prioritize the data-agnostic features.
papers.key_findings:
Incorporating data-agnostic features generally improves generalization performance, especially for short-form question answering datasets, but fails in some cases involving Commonsense Reasoning datasets.
Feature selection (retaining top-k hidden-state features) can amplify the contribution of data-agnostic features and yield additional gains, but the expected ordering of improvement does not always hold.
Analysis using SHAP values reveals that in successful cases, data-agnostic features are highly ranked, but in failure cases (e.g., with SWAG and Winogrande datasets) they are underweighted or sparsely ranked.
Probes trained solely on hidden-state features generalize poorly across tasks and datasets, indicating overfitting to dataset-specific features.
Factual QA and Reading Comprehension tasks show better cross-generalization, likely because their hidden-state representations are more similar, as suggested by PCA visualization.
papers.limitation:
The data-agnostic features were randomly selected without investigating whether all are effective or if including more/less would affect performance.
The rate of correct answers being misclassified when incorporating data-agnostic features is relatively high.
The baseline (without data-agnostic features) drifts slightly across the three probe configurations, introducing instability in comparisons.
The probe underweights data-agnostic features in Commonsense Reasoning datasets, suggesting their hidden states may already encode similar information.
future_direction: Systematically examine the effectiveness of individual data-agnostic features and the impact of including more or less of them.
Investigate the high rate of correct answers being misclassified when data-agnostic features are added.
Compare the proposed accuracy probe with the semantic entropy probe for generalization performance.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often generate responses that are factually incorrect yet expressed with high confidence, which can pose serious risks for end users. To address this, it is essential for LLMs not only to produce answers but also to provide accurate estimates of their correctness. Uncertainty quantification methods have been introduced to assess the quality of LLM outputs, with factual accuracy being a key aspect of that quality. Among these methods, those that leverage hidden states to train probes have shown particular promise, as these internal representations encode information relevant to the factuality of responses, making this approach the focus of this paper. However, the probe trained on the hidden states of one dataset often struggles to generalise to another dataset of a different task or domain. To address this limitation, we explore combining data-agnostic features with hidden-state features and assess whether this hybrid feature set enhances out-of-domain performance. We further examine whether selecting only the most informative hidden-state features, thereby discarding task-specific noise, enables the data-agnostic features to contribute more effectively. The experiment results indicate that although introducing data-agnostic features generally enhances generalisation performance in most cases, in certain scenarios their inclusion degrades performance. A similar pattern emerges when retaining only the most important hidden-state features - adding data-agnostic features does not consistently further enhance performance compared to using the full set of hidden-state features. A closer analysis reveals that, in some specific cases, the trained probe underweights the data-agnostic features relative to the hidden-state features, which we believe is the main reason why the results are inconclusive.

papers.title: The First to Know: How Token Distributions Reveal Hidden Knowledge in Large Vision-Language Models?
papers.research_question: Do models implicitly know that they are generating inappropriate or undesirable content?
papers.core_contribution: The logit distribution of the first token in LVLMs contains hidden knowledge that can be used via linear probing to detect inappropriate instructions and improve response generation.
papers.conclusion: Linear probing on the first token's logit distribution reveals hidden knowledge in LVLMs, enabling better detection of inappropriate instructions and improved response generation.
papers.key_findings:
The logit distribution of the first token contains sufficient information to determine if a model should respond to an instruction.
Hidden knowledge in logit distributions weakens as the model generates more tokens.
CLIP model shows strong performance on these tasks, suggesting dataset bias.
Linear probing on first logits improves performance on math correctness, object hallucination, and image classification tasks.
Finetuning LVLMs is less effective than linear probing for these tasks.
papers.limitation:
Dataset bias may simplify tasks, as CLIP performs well indicating distribution differences.
The decoding method sometimes leads to incorrect explanations.
papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs), designed to interpret and respond to human instructions, occasionally generate hallucinated or harmful content due to inappropriate instructions. This study uses linear probing to shed light on the hidden knowledge at the output layers of LVLMs. We demonstrate that the logit distributions of the first tokens contain sufficient information to determine whether to respond to the instructions, including recognizing unanswerable visual questions, defending against jailbreaking attacks, and identifying deceptive questions. Such hidden knowledge is gradually lost in logits of subsequent tokens during response generation. Then, we illustrate a simple decoding strategy at the generation of the first token, effectively improving the generated content. In experiments, we find a few interesting insights: First, the CLIP model already contains a strong signal for solving these tasks, which indicates potential bias in the existing datasets. Second, we observe performance improvement by utilizing the first logit distributions on three additional tasks, including indicating uncertainty in math solving, mitigating hallucination, and image classification. Last, with the same training data, simply finetuning LVLMs improves models' performance but is still inferior to linear probing on these tasks.
